Name: reasoning_recomputation_detection
Title: Do Reasoning Models Recompute What They Already Know? Detecting and Skipping Redundant Re-Derivation in Chain-of-Thought
Short Hypothesis: Long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces waste tokens by repeatedly re-deriving intermediate quantities the model has already computed and stored in its residual stream. These re-derivations are mechanistically detectable: the value is already linearly decodable from hidden states before it is re-verbalized. Detecting this 'already-known' signal online lets us skip redundant re-derivation steps, cutting tokens without retraining and with minimal accuracy loss.
Related Work: Training-based CoT compression (CRT's constrained optimization; GRACE's graph rationale distillation) reduces redundancy via post-training/SFT, requiring retraining and length-aware rewards. Prompt-based brevity and RL length penalties also require optimization or labels. Interpretability work on CoT (logit/tuned lens, activation patching) shows intermediate results are encoded internally but has not linked this to *recomputation* redundancy. My prior proposals target load-bearing token pruning and final-answer commitment. This proposal is distinct: it targets a specific, novel redundancy mechanism—re-derivation of already-encoded intermediate quantities—and turns a mechanistic 'already-known' probe into a training-free step-skipping controller, bridging interpretability with efficiency in a way no prior work does.
Abstract: Reasoning models generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, but a substantial share of tokens may re-derive intermediate quantities the model already computed earlier. We hypothesize that such re-derivation is mechanistically wasteful: the target quantity is already linearly decodable from the residual stream before the model re-verbalizes it. We test this by (1) segmenting CoT into reasoning steps and identifying intermediate values (numeric results, sub-conclusions), (2) training lightweight linear probes at step boundaries to predict whether a value the model is about to derive is already encoded in current hidden states, and (3) using activation patching to verify causally that the re-derivation adds little downstream information. We first characterize how often models recompute known quantities across GSM8K, MATH, and multi-hop logic (ProntoQA), and how this scales with CoT length and difficulty. We then build a training-free online controller: when the 'already-known' probe fires with high confidence at a step boundary, the controller injects the cached value and suppresses the redundant derivation, forcing the model to proceed. We evaluate accuracy-versus-tokens Pareto curves against full CoT, fixed truncation, and self-consistency truncation, plus a comparison to CRT-style trained compression. We expect 20-40% token reduction at near-equal accuracy and, as a scientific contribution, the first quantification of internal recomputation as a distinct source of CoT inefficiency, offering a mechanistic explanation for 'overthinking.'
Experiments: 1. Recomputation characterization: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, generate full CoT on GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA. Parse steps and extract intermediate quantities (numeric expressions via regex/AST for math; entity-relation sub-conclusions for logic). For each step that introduces a value, check via a linear probe on prior-step hidden states whether that value was already decodable; label such steps 'redundant re-derivation.' Report frequency and its correlation with CoT length and difficulty. 2. Causal validation: Use activation patching—replace the residual contribution of a flagged re-derivation span with a mean/ablated version and measure whether the final answer changes. Redundant steps should rarely change the answer. 3. Probe training: Train a lightweight linear/MLP 'already-known' probe on hidden states at step boundaries (labels from offline decodability + causal checks) to predict, online, whether the upcoming step is redundant. 4. Online skip controller: At each step boundary, run the probe; if it fires with confidence above threshold for a value that is decodable, inject a short cached statement ('We already have X = v') and continue generation, suppressing the redundant derivation. 5. Evaluation: accuracy vs. mean tokens generated (Pareto), wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, fixed truncation, self-consistency truncation, and a CRT-style trained-compression reference. Metrics: accuracy, tokens generated, probe AUC, fraction of steps skipped. 6. Ablations: probe layer, confidence threshold, math-only vs. logic transfer, cross-model probe transfer, and value-type breakdown (which quantities get recomputed most).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Segmenting CoT into steps and extracting intermediate values is noisy, especially for free-form reasoning; we restrict initial analysis to extractable numeric/entity values. 2. Some re-derivation may serve as verification/self-correction rather than pure redundancy; skipping it could hurt hard problems—the Pareto analysis and causal patching quantify this. 3. Linear decodability of a value does not guarantee the model would produce it correctly downstream; causal patching mitigates this. 4. Injecting cached values may distort generation dynamics; we test injection phrasing robustness. 5. Probes may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring per-setting calibration; we test transfer explicitly.
